entry.title: PHP2Shell makes runtime inventory the urgent patch problem
entry.summary:
PHP2Shell makes runtime inventory the urgent patch problem
PHP is often treated as a dependency of an application rather than an internet-facing runtime. The October 2026 PHP2Shell release shows why that distinction breaks down. Two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP interpreter can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution under the right conditions, and the affected component may be present in containers, shared hosting, serverless images, and long-lived virtual machines. The PHP project released fixes in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 on October 21, 2026. The two vulnerabilities are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both are relevant to web applications because the interpreter processes request data before the application's own authorization logic has any chance to run…

entry.summary: A dealer uploads a CSV with 500 rows. Each row is a SIM card that has to be activated on one of several carrier APIs, and each activation costs real wholesale money that you cannot get back if the row was bad. entry.title: Your minifier did not break your code. The missing semicolon did.
entry.summary:
Minification gets blamed for a lot of bugs it never caused. A script works fine in development, you run it through a minifier, and suddenly it throws in production. The minifier must have mangled something, right? Most of the time, no. The minifier just removed the whitespace that was secretly holding your code together. The real culprit is automatic semicolon insertion, and it was already in your code, waiting. JavaScript inserts semicolons for you when it thinks a statement has ended. That is convenient right up until a newline is the only thing separating two statements that should not be joined. Take this: const total = price + tax (total > 100 ? applyDiscount() : checkout())

entry.title: How to match business names and addresses to real places
entry.summary: Your CRM says "St Josephs Med Ctr, 1 Main". Your vendor file says "Saint Joseph's Medical Center, 1 Main Street, Suite 200". A franchise list says "Store #4127". Are these the same real place? Exact string matching says no. Fuzzy matching says maybe. You want to know which business actually exists, and where. Names come in with abbreviations, initialisms, store numbers, old spellings and "Inc" or "LLC" added or dropped. Addresses come in partial, with suite numbers in different fields, or as the registered office instead of the storefront. Comparing two strings can't tell you whether a business by that name really trades at that address today. The reliable approach is to resolve each record against evidence about the place itself: its own website, map listings, social profiles, registries.…
